record.final_answer:
Not fatal yet, but it is on a hard ceiling, and it's the kind of failure that only shows up on the night the tarball gets a bit bigger.

The numbers (scripts/upload.sh, CHUNK_MB=8):

  60 GiB at 8 MiB  -> 7,680 parts
  60 GB  at 8 MiB  -> 7,153 parts
  S3-compatible cap: 10,000 parts per multipart upload
  => 8 MiB parts can never carry more than 78.1 GiB, at any network speed

So today it passes, at ~72-77% of the part limit. Two consequences: the growth headroom is about one good week of data (a 78 GiB tarball simply cannot be uploaded — it fails with TooManyParts, which looks like a corrupt/truncated dump rather than a config limit), and you're burning ~7,000 signed PUTs per night instead of ~1,000, with ~7,000 chances for a retry and the per-request overhead on every one.

What I changed (scripts/upload.sh, now committed to working tree, not staged): the part size is derived from the file size instead of being fixed.

  - target 1,000 parts, floor 8 MiB (above the 5 MiB minimum a non-final part needs), rounded up to a multiple of 8 MiB
  - 60 GiB -> 64 MiB parts, 960 parts (ceiling becomes ~625 GiB)
  - small files still use 8 MiB, so nothing changes for them
  - CHUNK_MB=... in the environment still overrides, and a missing argument now fails with a usage line instead of an unbound-variable error

Verified with a stub corvane-cli on PATH (the real CLI isn't installed on this box, so this is logic + argument passing, not a live upload): 100 MiB -> 8MiB, 60 GiB -> 64MiB, 1 TiB -> 1056MiB, CHUNK_MB=32 honoured, no-arg case prints usage. `sh -n` clean.

Two things to confirm on your side:
  1. Corvane's documented part limit — I assumed the standard 10,000 / 5 GiB. Worth checking the gateway on stor-02 (logs in /var/log/corvane/) before trusting the 1,000-part target blindly.
  2. If the CLI buffers a whole part in memory, 64 MiB parts cost 64 MiB of RAM per concurrent part — fine here, but it's the reason I capped the target at 1,000 parts rather than making parts huge.

Not done: no retry/resume around the upload, and it still uploads the 60 GB tarball as one object. If you want, the next useful step is splitting the dump or adding `--resume`/retry behaviour, which matters more now than part size does.
